title: Like leaves
hook: Marcus recalls Homer: the generations of people are like leaves in the wind (Meditations 10.34)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Marcus told himself to stop talking about the good person and be one. Your line was be one. What good act did you do without a word? Day two hundred seventeen.

Walk down any street in autumn. The leaves come down in the wind, a few at a time, then all at once. You kick through them. By next spring the same trees will be full again, and none of the new leaves will know about the old ones. Now think about the people who were famous when your grandparents were young. The names everyone knew. How many could you name? Marcus kept a few lines from one of the oldest poems in Greek, and he turned to them to help him to remember something about fame, and loss, and time. Today: like leaves.
screen: `AUTUMN, AND THEN SPRING.` → `THE NAMES EVERYONE KNEW.` → `LIKE LEAVES.`

segments.voice: The lines come from Homer's Iliad. In the middle of the war at Troy, two warriors meet on the battlefield, and one asks the other who he is. The other answers, more or less: why ask about my family? The generations of people are like leaves. The wind scatters some on the ground, and the forest, when spring comes, grows others. So it is with people: one generation grows, another passes away. In Book Ten, Marcus says that for someone who has taken in the truth, even a short, familiar line like this is enough to free them from grief and fear. And then he applies it, one by one. Your children are leaves. The people who cheer you, and the ones who curse you or sneer behind your back, are leaves. The people who will carry your name and reputation after you're gone, leaves too. All of them come in spring, the wind brings them down, and the forest grows others in their place. That's heavy to hear. Marcus had buried several of his own children. He isn't saying they didn't matter. He's saying something about how to hold what matters: with open hands. This can sound cold. But leaves aren't worthless because they fall. All summer, the leaves feed the tree. Each one is beautiful in its season. It just doesn't last forever, and it was never meant to. Praise, insult, even fame after death, all leaves. What's left is how you live this season. Your line: like leaves.
screen: `A LINE FROM HOMER'S ILIAD.` · `THE WIND SCATTERS, THE FOREST GROWS.` · `PRAISE, INSULT, FAME: ALL LEAVES.` · then, large: `LIKE LEAVES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch leaves or grass move. If you can, look out a window, or step outside, and find leaves, grass, or even a plant on a shelf. If you can't, picture a tree in the wind. Just watch it move. Some leaves hold, some fall. Nothing is wrong. Let your breath move with it. The bell holds the time.
Like leaves. Marcus recalls Homer: people come and go like leaves in the wind, and the forest grows new ones in the spring. Today's word.
Your line: like leaves. Today, when praise or criticism comes your way, say the line, and let it fall as lightly as it came. Day two hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus often use short lines like this one, from poets and philosophers, as reminders of how briefly things last, to loosen the grip of praise, blame and fear.

fork.setup: you're a warrior at Troy, and an enemy asks about your family line. what does Homer's warrior say first?
options: why ask? people are like leaves.
fork.reveal: he says the generations are like leaves: the wind scatters them, and the forest grows new ones. then he tells his story anyway.

original.note: Greek: leaves. from Homer's line comparing the generations of people to leaves.

trapdoor: what you thought: life is short, so nothing matters.
what it means: people, praise and fame come and go like leaves, so hold them with open hands.
what a scholar hears: Iliad 6.146, Glaucus to Diomedes, one of the most quoted lines in Greek poetry, which Marcus adapts to children, critics and posthumous fame.

notes: Meditations 10.34 and Iliad 6.146ff are paraphrased; Long's rendering of the Homer lines was not certain enough to quote.
Confirm Marcus's application: children, those who praise or curse or sneer, those who pass on one's fame, all 'leaves', produced in spring and cast down by the wind.
Iliad 6: Glaucus answering Diomedes. The fork says he tells his story anyway, which he does at length. Confirm.
Marcus burying several children: confirm phrasing (many of his children died young).

Hook softened: 'the oldest poem in Greek' became 'one of the oldest poems in Greek' (the relative dating of the Iliad, Odyssey and Hesiod is debated), and 'Marcus loved' these lines became 'kept' (he quotes them once, in 10.34). Confirm.
Audit (2nd sample): fixed a pronoun slip in the teach ('the leaves ... It's beautiful in its season') so the line reads cleanly.
